A bicycle chain is composed of many moving metal parts—pins, rollers, and plates—that rub against each other thousands of times per ride. Lubricant creates a thin protective film between these surfaces, reducing friction and preventing metal-on-metal contact.

When a chain is left dry, this barrier disappears. The resulting friction causes the metal to grind away, physically stretching the chain (increasing "wear") and wearing down the teeth of the cassette and chainrings. This creates a destructive cycle: a worn chain fits poorly on the gears, accelerating the wear of the entire drivetrain.

A chain wears out faster when it's left dry because the links and rollers are designed to slide against each other with a thin film of lubricant in between. Without that film, the metal surfaces grind directly on one another, so friction and wear increase sharply. Every pedal stroke then shaves tiny amounts of metal off the pins and bushings, and the chain stretches out of spec sooner. Dry chains also trap grit and road film, which acts like sandpaper, and they're more prone to rust, which pits the surfaces and makes the wear even worse.

A dry chain wears faster because lubrication is what separates the moving parts. Inside each roller and pin, metal rides on metal. Oil forms a thin film that reduces friction and carries away heat. Without it, friction increases and the surfaces micro-weld and grind off each other with every pedal stroke.

Dirt makes it worse. A dry chain acts like sandpaper, pulling grit into the rollers and pins. That abrasive paste accelerates wear on the chain, cassette and chainrings, and it increases drivetrain drag.

What to tell customers:
* Clean and lube regularly, especially after wet or muddy rides
